div.p: Embodied agents powered by large language models (LLMs), such as Voyager, promise open-ended competence in worlds such as Minecraft. However, when powered by open-weight LLMs they still falter on elementary tasks after domainspecific fine-tuning. We propose MINDFORGE, a generative-agent framework for cultural lifelong learning through explicit perspective taking. We introduce three key innovations: (1) a structured theory of mind representation linking percepts, beliefs, desires, and actions; (2) natural inter-agent communication; and (3) a multi-component memory system. Following the cultural learning framework, we test MINDFORGE in both instructive and collaborative settings within Minecraft. In an instructive setting with GPT-4, MINDFORGE agents powered by open-weight LLMs significantly outperform their Voyager counterparts in basic tasks yielding 3× more tech-tree milestones and collecting 2.3× more unique items than the Voyager baseline. Furthermore, in fully collaborative settings, we find that the performance of two underachieving agents improves with more communication rounds, echoing the Condorcet Jury Theorem. MINDFORGE agents demonstrate sophisticated behaviors, including expert-novice knowledge transfer, collaborative problem solving, and adaptation to out-of-distribution tasks through accumulated cultural experiences. The code can be found at https://github.com/tapri-lab/mindforge.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: The development of generally capable agents marks a significant shift in advancing artificial intelligence, transitioning from assimilating data to generating novel knowledge through embodied interactions with open-ended environments [1][2][3][4]. Classical approaches leveraging reinforcement learning [5,6] and imitation learning [7] often struggle with generalization and exploration, as agents tend to converge on repetitive behaviors in static environments [8]. To address these limitations, researchers have sought to emulate human-like lifelong learning capabilities, developing systems that can continuously acquire, update, and transfer knowledge over extended periods [9,10].The advent of large language models (LLMs) has accelerated this pursuit, enabling the development of agents such as Voyager [11] that can apply internet-scale knowledge to continuously explore, plan, and acquire new skills in partially observable, open-ended environments such as Minecraft.

Despite their promise, we argue that state-of-the-art lifelong learning agents like Voyager face a crucial limitation: they learn in isolation, neglecting a fundamental aspect of human intelligence-the agents are able to find a solution through collaboration (actual in-game conversation excerpts) social context. So central is the social context to our existence that the Social Intelligence Hypothesis posits that our cognitive capabilities evolved primarily to navigate the complexities of social life [12,13]. This isolated learning becomes particularly problematic when coupled with these agents' reliance on closed LLMs like GPT-4. Wang et al. [11] note that "VOYAGER requires the quantum leap in code generation quality from GPT-4 which GPT-3.5 and open-source LLMs cannot provide". Our experiments (Section 5) corroborate this observation, demonstrating that replacing GPT-4 with open LLMs renders the Voyager agent incapable of even the most rudimentary tasks, such as collecting dirt in Minecraft. We ask: can an open LLM-powered agent, which struggles with basic tasks, improve through collaboration with others?

To address this question, we introduce the MINDFORGE framework, inspired by cultural learning, which contends that individuals internalize skills and strategies by observing others' perspectives, using Theory of Mind (ToM) to infer goals, beliefs, and intentions and thereby deepen social learning [14][15][16][17][18]. Our framework reframes knowledge distillation [19] as a social, test-time process: agents refine their beliefs through multi-turn dialogue with expert peers, without gradient updates. This interactive distillation supports test-time compute scaling [20], enabling agents to improve performance via communication, memory retrieval and perspective-taking. By structuring communication across turns, MINDFORGE also contributes to multi-turn LLM agent research [21,22], showing that open models can match GPT-4 through collaboration alone. Moreover, our analysis of weak-weak settings highlights a compute-performance tradeoff at inference, linking collaboration to test-time compute considerations [20].

Figure 1a provides an overview of our agents in action. Concretely, MINDFORGE extends Voyager by incorporating three key improvements: (1) perspective-taking through a causal ToM template [23] linking agent percepts, beliefs, desires, and actions; (2) a natural language communication interface between agents; and (3) memory updates following the Soar cognitive architecture [24], including semantic memory of task and environment-related knowledge and episodic memory.

Empirically, we instantiate MINDFORGE agents in Instructed Learning (mixed-expertise) and Collaborative Learning (matched-expertise) settings within the cultural learning framework [15]. MINDFORGE agents powered by open-weight LLMs outperform the original Voyager architecture [11] on two seemingly trivial tasks by more than 40%. We identify Voyager's specific failure cases:

(1) false beliefs and (2) code generation, and show how our method overcomes them through communication and perspective-taking. To assess lifelong learning, we run MINDFORGE on the Minecraft tech-tree and find that it surpasses open-weight Voyager variants in both key tech-tree milestones and the number of unique items obtained. Section 5.5 further shows that when both agents begin with the same limited capabilities, a single round of GPT-4 seeding followed by just seven turns of peer-to-peer dialogue lifts the population-level success rate from 62% to 79%, revealing a Condorcet-style "many-minds" boost that stems from richer interaction rather than larger models. This generalization in post-collaborative settings paves the way for agents that can continuously adapt through social interaction, reducing the reliance on large-scale computing resources for training and fine-tuning the underlying language models.

div.head: Related Work
div.p: Theory of Mind in Embodied Agents Early attempts to equip machines with mental-state reasoning drew on deep learning [25][26][27], reinforcement learning [28], and Bayesian models [29]. These systems were either confined to toy 2-D worlds [25,26] or failed to generalize to richer environments [27]. The emergence of large language models (LLMs) reignited interest in ToM, sparking evaluations of their putative capabilities [23,[30][31][32]. Although evidence so far suggests that LLMs lack genuine ToM, their breadth of knowledge has inspired a new wave of prompt-based frameworks [33][34][35][36]: the first two focus on perspective-taking, while the latter pair ground reasoning in explicit causal models. BIP-ALM remains the sole example that integrates such a framework with an LLM [37,38].

div.head: LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems
div.p: LLMs have demonstrated overwhelming success in performing a variety of single-agent tasks ranging from question answering and text generation to code synthesis and complex reasoning in embodied settings [11,39,40]. This success has started a growing interest in developing LLM-based multi-agent systems [21,22,[41][42][43], where language-based communication is a central component. For instance, CoELA [21] introduce a modular multi-agent framework that integrates memory, perception and execution, while COMBO [41] present a multi-agent cooperative framework, that deals with collaboration in partial egocentric views of the environment. However, these frameworks lack an explicit belief representation and Theory-of-Mind reasoning. Recently, benchmarks like MineCollab [44], designed for collaborative reasoning, find that current LLM agents are not suited for multi-agent collaboration in long-horizon embodied scenarios, a gap that MINDFORGE addresses by endowing agents with structured perspective taking capabilities.

div.head: Single-agent Frameworks
div.p: Recent research on long-horizon tasks in single-agent systems differs architecturally from MINDFORGE's unified collaborative learning framework. For example, Ex-peL [45] and CLIN [46] emphasize experiential learning through vectorized trajectories or causal abstractions but lack explicit belief graphs and integration across episodic, semantic, and procedural memories. Frameworks like DEPS [47] and ADaPT [48] enable in-episode self-correction via iterative refinement, yet insights are often ephemeral, confined to the context window without persistent storage or structured models of others' beliefs. SSO [49] provides procedural memory through skill libraries but omits episodic/semantic layers and social reasoning for targeted teaching or belief revision. Similarly, Adam [50] structures world knowledge as causal graphs in open environments, while Optimus-1 [51] builds hierarchical semantic graphs from experiences.

div.head: Background
div.p: Voyager Voyager agents consist of three main components: (1) an automatic curriculum generator, (2) a skill library, and (3) an iterative prompting mechanism. The automatic curriculum proposes progressively complex tasks, driving continuous learning. The skill library stores and retrieves learned behaviors, facilitating knowledge accumulation and transfer. The iterative prompting mechanism generates and refines executable code based on environmental feedback, allowing for adaptive behavior. Voyager demonstrated significant capabilities in item discovery, technology progression, and skill generalization. This system established a new benchmark in open-world AI agents, showcasing the potential for lifelong learning and adaptation in complex, dynamic environments. The Voyager framework serves as a base for our lifelong collaborative learning agents within Minecraft.

div.head: BigToM Causal Template
div.p: The BigToM causal template [23], provides a structured framework for representing Theory of Mind (ToM) scenarios as causal graphs. This template comprises key components including context, desire, percept, belief, causal event, and resulting actions. By representing ToM scenarios in this causal structure, the template allows for systematic manipulation of variables such as an agent's perceptions, beliefs, and actions in response to environmental changes. This approach enables the creation of diverse, well-controlled ToM scenarios, capturing the complex causal relationships between an agent's mental states and their behavior in social situations. The causal graph representation facilitates a more nuanced and systematic exploration of ToM reasoning, allowing for the examination of various inference patterns such as forward belief, forward action, and backward belief inferences in social cognitive tasks.

div.head: Method
div.p: To grant MINDFORGE agents the ability to learn through collaborative social interactions, we introduce the following components for communication and perspective-taking: (i) an explicit structured representation linking percepts, beliefs, desires, and actions (Section 4.1), (ii) perspective taking so that the agent can reason over self-beliefs and those about its collaborators (Section 4.2), (iii) a communication medium that the agents can use to share information in natural language (Section 4.3), and (iv) the ability to utilize different types of memory subsystems (Section 4.4).

div.head: Structured Representation of Own Mental States: Beliefs, Desires, and Intentions
div.p: For MINDFORGE agents to develop effective theory of mind capabilities, they must first possess structured representations of their own mental states. This explicit modeling of the self is crucial for recursive social reasoning: enabling agents not only to reason about their own beliefs, goals, perceptions, and how these might lead to their actions, but also to form a similar mental model for other agents. This mirrors findings in developmental psychology, where children first develop an awareness of their own thoughts, feelings, and goals before being able to infer the mental states of others [52,53]. This is further supported by neuroscientific research that has also identified distinct neural mechanisms for self-cognition and social cognition [54,55].

We draw on the classical Belief-Desire-Intention (BDI) framework [56] and operationalize it using the BigToM causal template (Section 3) [23]. In MINDFORGE, beliefs represent the agent's current understanding of the world inferred from sensory perception, including interactions with other agents. Desires encode the agent's goals, both generated by an automatic curriculum and those arising from collaborative interactions. Intentions correspond to concrete executable actions, implemented as generated code-and so, consistent with BigToM [23], we treat "intentions" and "actions" interchangeably in implementation. However, we note that this equivalence does not always hold conceptually: intentions refer to internal commitments or plans, while actions are observable behaviors that may diverge from intentions. For a deeper treatment of this distinction, see [57].

Belief Structure. We categorize a MINDFORGE agent's beliefs into four key categories, illustrated in Figure 3: i. perception-related beliefs, formed from direct sensory input via the Minecraft API; ii. task-related beliefs, inferred from the agent's reflection on its upcoming objectives; iii. interactionrelated beliefs, derived from chat messages during task execution; and iv. partner-related beliefs, which track others' mental states. Each belief type is generated via a separate LLM call, with prompts conditioned on current percepts, memory retrievals, and conversation history (see Section F). This modular belief formation feeds into the causal ToM template Figure 2a, which governs downstream action generation. Structured self-modeling thus serves as the foundation for cultural learning and perspective-taking.

div.head: Theory of Mind: Modeling Partner Perspectives
div.p: Building on the structured representation of their own mental states, MINDFORGE extend this modeling to others via Theory of Mind-the capacity to attribute beliefs, desires, and intentions to others. Each MINDFORGE agent achieves this by maintaining a partner-specific BigToM graph within its own beliefs, allowing it to reason about the internal state of each conversational partner

These representations guide how an agent interprets and responds to incoming communication.

During collaboration, an agent uses its internal model of its partner to simulate what the partner knows, believes, or needs. The underlying LLM receives this partner model along with the conversation history to generate responses incorporating the collaborator's point of view. As interaction proceeds, the partner beliefs are continuously updated using new received through the communication channel (Figure 6). This dynamic modeling of partner mental states endows MINDFORGE agents with one of the most crucial abilities within the cultural learning framework: reasoning about partner perspectives [14,15]. For instance, an expert agent can diagnose a novice's misconception and tailor its feedback accordingly, while a novice can ask more targeted questions with fewer digressions by simulating what the expert knows. See Section B.1 for more details on how perspective-taking is integrated into the communication module, and in-game examples.

div.head: Communication Medium
div.p: To take advantage of representations of each other's mental models and collaborate effectively, agents need to be able to communicate with each other. We operationalize communication in natural language, integrating the MINDFORGE framework's communication system with Minecraft's native in-game chat functionality. Specifically, once a MINDFORGE agent fails to complete a task, it initiates a communication round with its partner where it leverages its BigToM representation to ask for help. This system enables agents to exchange textual information and, crucially, to integrate feedback from collaborators directly into their belief systems. Concretely, we utilize the Mineflayer API [58] to extract and process chat data from the Minecraft environment. By leveraging the game's existing chat system, the framework ensures that collaborative interactions occur in a context-appropriate manner, closely mirroring human-to-human communication within Minecraft.

To handle the resulting conversation, we use a dedicated LLM instance within the MINDFORGE agent which is tasked with synthesizing and interpreting the conversation into the structured BigTOM BDI template, generating both interaction beliefs and partner beliefs (see prompts in Section F). This instance does not directly influence any other parts of the agent.

div.head: Memory Subsystems
div.p: A MINDFORGE agent's memory consists of three subsystems drawing on research about human memory: (i) episodic, (ii) semantic, and (iii) procedural memory.

Episodic memory deals with pertinent information about the agent's past attempts at a task and social interactions with other agents. Recollections of past episodes serve as context for humans to interpret others' behaviors, leading to divergent future actions in the same situation in response to different recollections [59]. Humans also tend to summarize information from their social interactions, but at the same time are capable of preferentially accessing episodes when the credibility of certain summaries is low due to the lack of evidence [60]. Moreover, findings also suggest that there are processes in the brain for updating these summaries as new episodes transpire [60,61]. Inspired by complementary learning systems theory, Larimar [62] enhances LLMs with a distributed episodic memory module, enabling dynamic knowledge updates without any gradient-based learning. Furthermore, Optimus-1 integrates past experiences in a multimodal memory storage mechanism and abstracted experience pool used for summarization of past experiences. For a MINDFORGE agent, the role of episodic memory is twofold. Firstly, it stores details about its partners revealed during previous conversations that can be exploited for perspective-taking in future communication.

Secondly, we store past actions that led to failure and retrieve them based on their similarity with the task at hand. Thus, a MINDFORGE agent can track both the progress of its partner and learn from past failures.

Semantic memory constitutes an individual's store of knowledge about the world. The content of semantic memory is abstracted from the experience and is therefore said to hold summarized generalizations, likely without references to specific experiences [60,61,63]. For a MINDFORGE agent, the semantic memory stores information related to the task and environment. It stores information relevant to completing a task; for instance, the prerequisites for being able to mine dirt in the game world. Such a piece of information is not necessarily tied to one specific episode. Rather, it is generally useful information about the world and can be distilled from the episodic memory.

Finally, procedural memory stores the skills that the agent learns and is analogous to the skill library present in the original Voyager framework [11]. The skills stored in the procedural memory are reusable pieces of code that the agent can use for solving problems, allowing the agent to take on more complex tasks while avoiding re-learning elements previously used successfully. As illustrated in Figure 2a, episodic and semantic memory stores influence the agent's beliefs, while procedural memory provides the routines that inform the agent's next action. Additional information about the memory subsystems can be found in Section B.2, where we provide implementation details, and an ablation for the episodic memory component, where we show that omitting it from MINDFORGE leads to a drop in success rate.

div.head: Experimental Setup
div.p: Our MINDFORGE framework introduces three advances that let agents improve continuously through social exchange: (1) explicit theory-of-mind representations for reasoning about peers, (2) Naturallanguage dialogue for coordination, and (3) integrated semantic and episodic memory to retain experience. We evaluate these additions in the same Minecraft world used by Voyager [11], built on MineDojo [64] with motor control via Mineflayer [58]. Component LLMs communicate through DSPy [65,66] and LangChain [67] for generation and embedding. In the base experimental setting, we follow Voyager [11] and allow the agent to execute 4 sequential actions to solve a task. MINDFORGE agents that interact (see Section 5.3) interleave one communication round (via the in-game chat) between two environmental actions. A snapshot of this setup can be seen in Figure 4a. For isolated tasks we measure the fraction of successes over 24 independent trials (one task per trial). In techtree experiments we follow Voyager's protocol, tracking milestone achievements and unique items collected. To ensure comparability, we preserve Voyager's original prompt structure and workflow throughout.

div.head: Voyager With Open-Weight LLMs
div.p: To establish non-interactive performance baselines, we replace GPT-4 [68] with three open-weight LLMs in the Voyager framework [11]: Mistral-7B [69], Mixtral-8x7B [70], and Llama 3.1-8B [71], selected for their long context windows and manageable size. Testing focuses on two fundamental Minecraft tasks: collecting single blocks of dirt and wood. Results in Table 1 reveal that while GPT-4 achieves perfect performance, open-weight LLMs struggle significantly even with these basic tasks without collaboration. This aligns with Wang et al. [11]'s observation that GPT-4's superior code generation capabilities enable it to obtain 5.7× more unique items than other models, establishing a clear baseline for measuring the impact of our collaborative approach.

Fine-Tuning Does Not Help Parameter-efficient tuning often helps LLMs [72], yet adapting Mistral-7B with GPT-4 execution traces (reasoning + code) and Minecraft manuals (domain knowledge; Section E) produced no benefit. In cultural-learning terms [14,15] this is imitation learning, but the tuned model still scores 7% on dirt collection (±0) and 12.5% on wood collection (+8.5) as shown in Table 1. Post-hoc analysis shows the tuning makes outputs wordier, blurs decisionmaking, and erodes instruction-following, indicating that naively imitating unstructured traces is counter-productive.

div.head: Introducing Collaboration: MINDFORGE Agents
div.p: Having shown that PEFT-based imitation learning fails to improve agent capabilities, we evaluate our proposed MINDFORGE framework. We adopt an instructive learning approach within the cultural learning framework [15], where an expert agent guides a novice through communication and perspective-taking. This multi-agent collaboration effectively bridges the performance gap between open-weight LLMs and GPT-4, addressing the failure cases identified in Figure 4.

div.head: Feasibility: Human (Expert) Collaboration Improves Performance
div.p: To establish feasibility, we first conduct a wizard-of-oz study where a human expert interacts with an open-weight LLM-powered MINDFORGE agent through the in-game chat. div.head: GPT-4 (Expert) Collaboration Maintains Performance Benefits
div.p: We replace the human expert with a GPT-4-powered MINDFORGE agent that collaborates with an open-weight LLM agent. The expert agent infers its partner's failure cases through perspective-taking based on natural language communication in the game chat. Unlike human collaboration, agents cannot directly access each other's internal beliefs and must rely on Theory of Mind through communication to model their counterpart's mental state. This perspective-taking enables the expert to accurately diagnose and address the weaker agent's misconceptions. Notably, this setup generalizes the classic notion of knowledge distillation beyond logits or model weights: here, distillation unfolds through social interaction, where the expert agent transmits structural knowledge, corrects false beliefs, and shapes the student's internal representations in real time. As shown in Table 2, this approach significantly improves performance compared to the non-interactive baselines, achieving on average a 16.1% increase in task completion rates for dirt collection and a 13% increase for wood collection tasks respectively. A sample conversation can be found in Section D.

div.head: Ablations
div.p: To elucidate the MINDFORGE framework's components, we conducted targeted ablations. The perspective-taking module, enabling agents to reason over partners' beliefs, boosts task completion by up to 13%, as evidenced by comparisons across multiple communication rounds (see Table 7, Section B.1). Our structured ToM representation outperforms its unstructured variant in complex Minecraft tasks (Table 8). Additionally, ablating the episodic memory component reveals that retaining past failures enhances performance (Table 9, Section B.2).

div.head: More Communication Rounds Improve Performance
div.p: Since communication is central to our framework, we examine the benefits of multiple rounds per task trial, assessing communication and perspective-taking amid escalating opportunities. We pair a GPT-4 MINDFORGE expert with a Mixtral-8x7B MINDFORGE weak agent. Figure 5 demonstrates communication's value through a sharp rise in task completion rates with additional rounds, while Figure 6 illustrates the expert's progressively accurate grasp of the partner's mental state. Further evidence in Section A.1 affirms communication's importance in instructive and collaborative settings, even for demanding Minecraft tasks ("Craft a pickaxe" and "Mine Iron") involving MINDFORGE agents.

div.head: MINDFORGE Lifelong Learning
div.p: We evaluate MINDFORGE's lifelong learning capabilities against both GPT-4 and open-weight Voyager [11] variants. The progression through increasingly complex technological achievements (from wooden to diamond tools) provides a rigorous test-bed for assessing lifelong learning and collaboration abilities of MINDFORGE. We follow the methodology from Voyager and evaluate performance on three key milestones: (1) wooden tools, (2) stone tools and (3) iron tools.

In line with the findings in Table 1, Table 3 highlights the performance gap between GPT-4 powered Voyager and its open-weight variants, with only Llama 3.1-70B [71] reaching the wooden tools milestone. On the other hand, MINDFORGE shows substantial improvement across the board both in terms of achieved milestones and efficiency (number of iterations). Notably, Llama 3.1-70B [71] powered MINDFORGE achieves two additional tech-tree milestones, nearing the performance with the original GPT-4 powered Voyager [11]. We observe a steady increase in efficiency (number of iterations) as the size of the LLM increases: Llama 3.1-70B [71] powered MINDFORGE is 1.62× more efficient than its Llama 3.1-8B counterpart for reaching the wooden tools milestone, suggesting that larger models can better utilize the collaborative learning framework. Furthermore, to understand the impact of collaboration in a mixed-expertise collaborative setting, we experiment with a noncollaborative MINDFORGE ablation. Notably, MINDFORGE agents without collaboration require on average 15 more prompting iterations to reach the wooden tools milestone and 34 iterations to reach the stone tools milestone. Thus, the collaborative framework not only enhances task completion rates but also enables more efficient acquisition of complex skills. We further test the generalization capabilities of MINDFORGE agents in Section A.2 where we show how even after collaboration finishes, the agents can reuse the knowledge in out-of-distribution tasks.

div.head: MINDFORGE Collaborative Learning Setting
div.p: While prior sections focused on instructive learning from stronger peers, we now consider a more challenging setup: collaboration between two MINDFORGE agents of matched capabilities, each powered by the same type of open-weight LLM. This setting reflects mutual cultural learning without access to an expert where the agents must bootstrap improvements solely through interaction, thereby mimicking certain qualities of emergence. Critically, we evaluate not individual trajectories, but instead focus on population-level performance: after N rounds of communication, what fraction of agent pairs from the total pool succeed in completing the task? As shown in Table 2, when agents begin from unprimed states, collaboration often leads to stagnation or even degradation which mirrors the "blind leading the blind" dynamic, where flawed mental models are mutually reinforced.

However, even minimal prior expert instruction-such as a single round of GPT-4-guided collaboration-can prime agents for more effective peer interaction, even if they still fail when acting alone. As shown in Figure 7, we pair Mixtral-8x7B agents that each received N communication rounds of GPT-4 guided trial before interacting. We observe that the fraction of successful agents steadily increases with additional communication rounds between themselves (Mixtral agents). From a 62% baseline population succeeding, we reach 79% of the population succeeding after seven turns, showing a 17% increment. This result reflects a form of test-time compute scaling, where richer interaction, not larger models, drives the emergent improvements across the group.

This also aligns with the Condorcet Jury Theorem [73], which predicts that collective decisions improve when individuals exceed a baseline level of competence. Here, we see a distributed variant of this principle in action: once agents cross a minimal competence threshold, the communication induced bootstrapping can yield reliable gains at the population level.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: The MINDFORGE framework demonstrates that cultural learning can overcome the limitations of open-weight LLMs in embodied environments. Integrating theory of mind, natural communication, and structured memory systems enables MINDFORGE agents to learn from both mixed and matched expertise peers and overcome fundamental failure modes in perception and code generation. Our experiments show that collaboration significantly improves performance on lifelong learning scenarios, with agents collecting 2.3× more unique items and achieving 3× more tech-tree milestones when paired with expert agents. Crucially, in the collaborative setting, we show that the fraction of successful agents scales as a function of communication rounds; revealing emergent gains through perspective taking and interaction. These results suggest that social learning could reduce embodied AI's dependence on large proprietary models, opening new paths for democratized agent development aligned with Green AI principles [74].

div.head: NeurIPS Paper Checklist
div.p: 1. Claims Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the paper's contributions and scope? Answer: [Yes] Justification: We back up the claims made in the abstract and introduction in Section 5, where we run extensive experiments in Minecraft and show the benefits of the proposed framework. Furthermore, we offer qualitative results through various figures and text snippets in the manuscript. These are available in the main paper as well as in the appendix (e.g. Section D).
Guidelines:

• The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including the contributions made in the paper and important assumptions and limitations. A No or NA answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers.
• The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings.
• It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals are not attained by the paper.

div.head: Limitations

• The answer NA means that the paper has no limitation while the answer No means that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper.
• The authors are encouraged to create a separate "Limitations" section in their paper.

• The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be.

• The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on a few datasets or with a few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated.
• The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach.

For example, a facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or a speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon.
• The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size.
• If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to address problems of privacy and fairness.

• While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by reviewers as grounds for rejection, a worse outcome might be that reviewers discover limitations that aren't acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an important role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. div.head: B.2 Memory Components
div.p: MINDFORGE employs three types of memory subsystems, as discussed in Section 4.4. These components ensure that the agent can reuse and recall relevant information about the task it is trying to complete from past experiences and interactions with other agents. The importance of procedural memory with respect to task completion is already studied in [11], concluding that reusing previous code snippets becomes increasingly important with the difficulty of the tasks. To understand the effect of episodic memory in the MINDFORGE framework, we perform an ablation on the episodic memory component within two Minecraft tasks. Table 9 showcases the drop in completion rate without the use of the episodic memory component. While we do not consider the tech-tree experiments here, we expect that considering past failure episodes leads to increasingly better results. 8 showcases how perspective-taking integrates with the overall communication mechanism.

div.head: Update internal representation
div.p: Take Perspective Once the agent receives a message in the Minecraft chat, a first LLM call is executed where the agent updates the stateful internal representation about the agent that sent the message. This update process is shown in Figure 6. Subsequently, the updated internal representation is used as context together with the rest of the conversation to take perspective of the situation of the other MINDFORGE agent. Similar to the first stage, perspective-taking is implemented as a LLM call, with the following prompt: Prompt for perspective-taking You are a Minecraft agent named {{name}} and you are having a conversation with another agent named {{other_name}}.

div.head: C.2 Episodic Memory
div.p: We implement episodic memory as a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) using LangChain [67]. Specifically, we embed all the episodes where the agent failed to complete the task using text-embedding-ada-002. An episode consists of the context used to generate the action, the code itself and the corresponding critic message. Subsequently, when the agent generates a new action, the RAG is queried to retrieve the k=5 most relevant failure episodes with respect to the task at hand. Lastly, to ensure we do not populate the context window with too many tokens, we generate a summary (using an LLM) of the retrieved episodes and feed this summary in the context used to generate the action. Below you can find the corresponding prompts for generating the episodic summary: System message You are a helpful assistant tasked with summarizing past experience episodes and pointing out the causes of failure. Create a concise summary.

div.head: Prompt message
div.p: Please summarize these episodes and why they failed:{combined_episodes}

div.head: C.3 Procedural Memory
div.p: The procedural memory has an identical design and functionality with the skill library introduced in Voyager [11]. Once a task gets successfully completed, we store the corresponding piece of code such that we can later reference it in adjacent tasks. This becomes increasingly important in tasks that require multiple steps, like crafting a pickaxe: the agent needs to first create a crafting table, create wooden sticks and only then attempt to craft the pickaxe. When we run the MINDFORGE framework in an open-ended setting, the procedural memory allows the agent to continuously evolve and create an increasingly large collection of reusable skills.

div.head: C.4 Semantic Memory
div.p: As described in Section 4.4, semantic memory stores certain beliefs the agent has about the environment, coming from experience with the environment and the other MINDFORGE agents. Whenever MINDFORGE attempts a new task, it creates a certain belief about how the task should be solved. For example, the agent might believe it requires tools to mine a block of dirt. This belief is then added to the context of the LLM when the environment action is generated. As highlighted in Section 1, one of the primary failure cases of Voyager are the false beliefs that come from this LLM generation. However, compared to Voyager [11], we leverage the communication with other MINDFORGE agents such that these beliefs get updated and refined. Below we showcase an example of false belief correction when trying to collect a block of wood: Initial belief inside the semantic memory {"How to mine 1 wood log in Minecraft?": "Answer: To mine 1 wood log in Minecraft, you need to use an axe."} Updated belief after communication {"How to mine 1 wood log in Minecraft?": "Answer: To mine 1 wood log in Minecraft, you need to punch a tree with your bare hands."} In addition to task-related memory, the MINDFORGE agent maintains a stateful set of beliefs about the other agents in the environment that are constantly updated across episodes. An example of this is presented in Figure 6, where the agent updates its representation based on the contents of the conversation. Thus, keeping track of various information and facts about other MINDFORGE agents acts as a semantic memory retrieval when agents communicate.

div.head: D Sample Conversation
div.p: Each communication round between two MINDFORGE agents comprises of six sending messages in a turn-based manner through the Minecraft build-in chat. Below you can find a sample conversation showcasing how the expert agent (Strong) helps the weak (Weak) agent.
Conversation about completing the task: "Mine 1 wood log" Weak: Hey, can you help me with Mine 1 wood log?

Strong: Absolutely, I can help you with that. Given your current location in the dark forest biome and the presence of dark oak logs around you, you should be able to mine a log without any issues. Here's the code you can use: 'mine('dark_oak_log')'. This command will make your agent mine a dark oak log. Just make sure you are close enough to the tree when executing this.

Weak: Thank you for the helpful guidance, Strong! However, in my case, I am currently in a dark forest biome as well, but I am having trouble finding a tree during the night. Could you suggest a way to find a tree during the day so I can mine the wood log? I also noticed that I don't have a wooden axe in my inventory, so I may need to craft one before attempting to mine the log. I appreciate your assistance in this matter.

Strong: Of course, I understand your predicament. Since it's currently night time, visibility might be low which makes it challenging to locate a tree. You can wait until daybreak for better visibility. Use the 'wait_until_day()' function to wait until it's daytime. For crafting a wooden axe, you would need 3 wood planks and 2 sticks. You can obtain wood planks from a wood log by using the 'craft('wooden_plank', wood_log)' command and sticks from 2 wooden planks using the 'craft('stick', wooden_plank)' command. Once you have these, you can craft a wooden axe using the 'craft('wooden_axe', wooden_plank, stick)' function.

Here's the code: ''' wait_until_day() craft('wooden_plank', wood_log) craft('stick', wooden_plank) craft('wooden_axe', wooden_plank, stick) ''' Once you have your axe and it's day time, you should be able to easily locate and mine a tree for the wood log.
Weak: Thank you, Strong. I appreciate your help.

div.head: E Fine-tuning setup E.1 Execution Logs
div.p: For the first fine-tuning variant, we use execution logs generated by a Voyager agent powered by GPT-4. Specifically, these logs contain input and output text information obtained from the components specific to the architecture, such as the actor or the critic. We find this to be a meaningful way to transfer knowledge as well as reasoning capabilities from GPT-4 to Mistral-7B. To perform the fine-tuning, we use LoRA [75] due to its low computational requirements.

div.head: E.2 Wiki Data and Documentation
div.p: The second fine-tuning variation we consider builds upon the initial setup presented above and incorporates more structured information about Minecraft by including the Minecraft Wiki [64] and Minecraft API documentation. Similar to the first variant we use LoRA [75].

div.head: MindForge: Empowering Embodied Agents with Theory of Mind for Lifelong Cultural Learning Appendices
A.1 Collaborative Experiments
div.p: We provide an extended set of experiments to reinforce our findings in Figure 5 and Figure 7. Specifically, we consider atomic tasks that are significantly harder than dirt and wood collection in order to demonstrate the generality of our framework: (1) mining an iron block and (2) crafting a wooden pickaxe. As Table 4 shows, extend communication and perspective-taking between MINDFORGE agents enable significant improvements on complex Minecraft tasks that require compositionality (41% → 62% and 20% → 45%). Similarly to Figure 7, we see that a purely collaborative setting results in smaller performance gains (20% → 33%) than instructive learning, due to reinforcing wrong beliefs and similar thinking patterns.

div.head: A.2 Post-Collaboration and OOD tasks
div.p: Do social interactions have long-term effects on agents and help them perform better on different tasks? We consider the impact of interactions in post-collaboration and out-of-distribution scenarios to assess MINDFORGE's generalization and lifelong learning capabilities. Specifically, we define postcollaboration scenarios as a non-collaborative setting where the MINDFORGE agent tries to complete a task based on prior beliefs formed from a previous collaborative experience stored in the semantic memory. Moreover, we consider scenarios where the agent is tasked with solving a novel task with prior collaborative experience on an adjacent task in the Minecraft tech-tree. As Table 5 shows, collaboration between MINDFORGE agents together with semantic memory showcase an average improvement of 8.33% for in-distribution tasks (dirt collection) together with an average improvement of 8.78% in non-collaborative out-of-distribution scenarios (wood collection). These results showcase the importance of semantic memory in achieving continual learning through collaboration.

div.head: A.3 Alternative Communication Protocols
div.p: Table 6 shows the performance of MINDFORGE agents when they are allowed to begin a conversation at point compared to when they can only initiate a conversation upon failure.

div.head: B Additional Ablations B.1 Perspective Taking
div.p: To quantitatively assess the effect of perspective-taking, we perform an ablation study where we attempt to solve a Minecraft task without perspective-taking during communication in an instructive learning setting. Table 7 showcases how the absence of perspective-taking leads to worse performance, irrespective of how much agents communicate. Moreover, as the agents use more communication rounds when trying to solve a task, taking perspective of the other's agent situation increases taskcompletion rate. We attribute the positive correlation between performance and usage of perspective-taking during communication to the ability of the MINDFORGE agent to provide more relevant and directed advice. This observation is also supported by the substantial increase in performance in the first two rounds as presented in Table 7, where the teacher agent provides more insightful information as it gets to know the other's agent situation better.

Additionally, we further ablate our structured representation of Theory of Mind by considering an unstructured perspective-taking 2-step prompt presented in Think Twice [33]. Table 8 showcases that a structured ToM representation provides a meaningful advantage on complex Minecraft tasks.
